verdicts.summary: Hosted decision after a renewed token: the decision's CSRF check uses the renewed session id. If renewal changes that id, Approve dead-ends on 'Enter a pairing code instead' with no code field on the hosted page. Whether renewal changes the id depends on relay token minting, which is not in this checkout.
verdicts.missing: Relay-side renewal: whether a renewed DPoP access token keeps the same sessionId claim. Scenario if it does not: the consent page stays open past the access-token lifetime, Approve triggers renewal, the CSRF comparison at McpOAuth.ts:474 fails, and the user sees 'Your session cannot approve this request. Enter a pairing code instead.' on a page with no code field.

verdicts.summary: The 10 s bound covers renewal, request and the one retry. The first authorizeDpopHttp is outside it but renewal is capped at 30 s, so no unbounded spinner. A timed-out decision after the server approved only loses the redirect; a retry mints a fresh one-use code.
verdicts.scenario: Relay renewal stalls on the retry path. The loop at environmentHttpAuth.ts:183-259 sits inside the timeoutOrElse at 260-271, so the stall ends in RemoteEnvironmentAuthTimeoutError, which connectMcpApproval.ts:109 maps to the retryable ConnectMcpApprovalUnavailableError. Renewal in service.ts:445-454 is capped at 30 s.

verdicts.summary: Making headers optional is safe on both sides. A cookie caller sending headers {} falls back to the cookie, and PeerLinks sends a pairing-code decision, which never reaches the session check.
verdicts.scenario: ConnectAgentSurface sends headers {} with a cookie and no Authorization header, so resolveRequestCredential (EnvironmentAuth.ts:762-769) takes the cookie as before. PeerLinks sends headers {} with a pairing-code decision; approve() takes the pairing-code branch (McpOAuth.ts:450-469) and never calls approvingSession.

verdicts.summary: The 'peer links stay on the environment page and need a code' claim is false. On the environment's own page a peer-link client gets a browser-session one-click, because neither approvingSession nor approve() checks peerLink for browser sessions. Only pairing-code decisions are blocked.
verdicts.scenario: 1) Linked environments is on, so anyone can register a peer-link client on the tunnel host with redirect https://attacker.example/cb (register has no auth; peerLink is set when software_id matches, McpOAuth.ts:343-355). 2) The victim opens /authorize with that client_id. The server sends peer links to /connect-agent (mcpOAuthHttp.ts:128-133). 3) The page loads with csrfToken and oneClickAccess from the victim's cookie session (approvingSession has no peerLink check). 4) Approve sends a browser-session decision, which approve() accepts with no peerLink check (McpOAuth.ts:470-481). The code is minted with peerLink true (McpOAuth.ts:435), so the victim grants a link with one click instead of typing a pairing code.

verdicts.summary: The flag is set unconditionally (ServerEnvironment.ts:292) and read only by the wizard (UseInAnotherAppDialog.tsx:125-126). Whether the failure mode happens depends on whether the hosted app at the configured URL serves /approve-agent, which is outside this checkout. The nightly host part is finding 2.
verdicts.missing: The deployed hosted app at DEFAULT_HOSTED_APP_URL and at https://nightly.app.t3.codes: whether it serves the /approve-agent route built from this commit. The route exists in this checkout (apps/web/src/routes/approve-agent.tsx), so the risk is deployment only.

verdicts.summary: The client accepts a superset of the server's loopback rule, so it refuses no redirect the server registers. Bracketed IPv6 works because URL.hostname keeps the brackets.
verdicts.scenario: Register http://[::1]:53682/cb. The server accepts it (hostname '[::1]' is in LOOPBACK_HOSTNAMES, McpOAuth.ts:60). The client's agentRedirectUrl parses hostname '[::1]' and isLoopbackHost matches it via the explicit check, so the redirect is allowed. Other server-registrable hosts are only localhost and 127.0.0.1, which the client also accepts.

verdicts.summary: Approve is gated by loaded status, armed, pending and a non-null decision. Stale loads are dropped by the cancelled flag. A double-click can send two decisions, but each mints its own one-use code, so the second is harmless.
verdicts.scenario: Switch windows and come back during consent: the focus handler rearms and Approve stays disabled for 700 ms. A stale load answer after an effect cleanup is ignored. A decision with a non-redirect answer clears pending and shows an error.

verdicts.summary: Only https, or http on a loopback host, is followed. The server only emits registered URIs, which are https or loopback http, so legitimate redirects pass. javascript: and data: are refused and shown as an error.
verdicts.scenario: A decision or load answer carries javascript:alert(1) or data:text/html,... : followRedirect returns false and the page shows UNSAFE_REDIRECT. A registered https callback or loopback callback: followRedirect navigates. Server redirects are built only from validated redirect URIs (redirectMatches at McpOAuth.ts:119-128).

verdicts.summary: Finding 4's concern is not reachable. Under a managed policy that denies remote clients, T3 Connect's connector never runs, so there is no tunnel hostname for the hosted redirect and the wizard's open gate (which needs a tunnel probe) never opens. The hosted wizard therefore only runs where the policy allows remote clients.
verdicts.scenario: Policy has clients without 'remote'. allowsConnect is false (managedLimits.ts:75-77), so connectAllowed is false and no connector runs (ManagedEndpointRuntime.ts:215-216). No tunnelHostname exists, so hostedApprovalUrl returns none (mcpOAuthHttp.ts:81) and the wizard shows GateScreen, not ConnectStep (UseInAnotherAppDialog.tsx:144). Residual: connectAllowed is read once at startup, so a policy edited at runtime is not re-checked here. That is pre-existing and not part of this change. The server does refuse pairing-link creation under this policy (EnvironmentAuth.ts:1061-1066), but I did not confirm that the MCP code route goes through it.

verdicts.summary: Every call result becomes a Result: success passes the answer on, and failures become a user message. Non-unavailable failures show the generic 'Could not reach this environment. Try again.' No failure is silently treated as success.
verdicts.scenario: A rejected or timed-out command: runConnectMcpApproval returns Result.fail(squashed). connectTransport maps isUnavailable to its message, or else the generic message. A successful answer with a redirect or refusal is handled in the switch at ApproveAgentSurface.tsx:54-62.

verdicts.summary: Phishing on the trusted hosted domain. Any visitor can register a non-peer client on a tunnel host without auth. A link to that host's /authorize redirects the owner to app.t3.codes/approve-agent with the owner's environment id. The owner signs in to T3 Connect and clicks Approve, granting the attacker's client access. The consent page shows the attacker's name and redirect host, with a warning.
verdicts.scenario: 1) Attacker POSTs /oauth/mcp/register on victim's tunnel host with a name like 'T3 Code' and redirect https://attacker.example/cb (no auth; not a peer link). 2) Attacker sends victim https://<tunnel>/authorize?...&client_id=<attacker>. 3) The server redirects to app.t3.codes/approve-agent?environment=<id>&... (mcpOAuthHttp.ts:127-135). 4) Victim signs in to T3 Connect on the trusted domain and clicks Approve. The code is redirected to the attacker's URI. The pre-change flow needed the tunnel origin, and the code path needed a code.
